title: What Does a Consistent Ethic of Life Look Like?
subtitle: The dignity of the unborn, the aged, the disabled, and the dying, and what a consistent ethic of life requires of us.
question: If every human being bears the image of God, why is it that each of us reaches so quickly to decide which lives at the edges still count?
whyItMatters: The edges are where a society confesses what it actually believes. Not the strong adult in the middle of his powers, who can defend himself and pay his own way, but the one who cannot. The child too small to be seen. The old man who no longer remembers your name. The woman on the gurney whose body has stopped cooperating. The man on death row whose crime is real and whose face we would rather not see. We have learned to measure a life by what it produces, and at the edges production falls to nothing, and so at the edges the measuring becomes a kind of permission. This is the most politically charged question in this section, and I will not pretend otherwise. People carry wounds here that no argument can reach. I have sat with the woman weeping over an abortion she chose at nineteen and the woman weeping over one she was pressured into and the woman who lost a child she desperately wanted, and I will not let an argument trample any of them.
biblicalFoundation:
Scripture does not begin with our usefulness. It begins with our origin. The first thing said over the human being is that he is made in the image of God, male and female, and that image is not earned by capacity or revoked by its loss. The unborn child, the man with advanced dementia, the infant born with a body that will not carry her long, all of them bear it. The image is not a reward for performance. It is the ground we stand on before we have done anything at all.

The Psalmist does not speak of the womb as a waiting room. He says, you knit me together in my mother's womb, I am fearfully and wonderfully made, your eyes saw my unformed body. And to Jeremiah the Lord says, before I formed you in the womb I knew you. Knowing precedes forming. The relationship is older than the body. This is not a verse to be wielded as a weapon. It is a window into how God regards the smallest among us, before they can speak, before they can be wanted, before they can be useful to anyone.

The sixth word given at Sinai is plain. You shall not murder. But the same Law that guards life at its beginning guards it at its other edges with the same insistence. Rise in the presence of the gray head, it says, and honor the face of the old man. Defend the weak and the fatherless, uphold the cause of the poor and the oppressed. The God who forbids the shedding of the child's blood is the God who commands that the alien among you be loved as yourself, for you were aliens in Egypt. The Law does not let us pick.

And then Jesus collapses the whole question into a single sentence that gives no tribe a place to hide. Whatever you did for the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me. The hungry, the stranger, the naked, the sick, the prisoner. He stands with the condemned man in his cell and the starving child in the camp and the unborn life that cannot yet cry out. He has placed himself at every edge we are tempted to abandon. To set aside any of them is to set aside him.

churchRecord.led: When Rome left unwanted infants exposed on hillsides to die of cold or be taken by beasts, it was Christians who went out at night and carried them home. When plague emptied the cities and the well fled, the church stayed to nurse the dying, and many died doing it. The hospice, the orphanage, the leper colony, the first hospitals, these grew from a people who believed the dying and the abandoned still bore the face of God. For long centuries the church was the only institution that would gather up the lives everyone else had written off.
churchRecord.failed: But the same church has again and again been selective and harsh. It has defended the unborn on Sunday and turned a cold face to the poor mother on Monday, offering her judgment where it owed her bread. It has been silent before the lynching tree and comfortable beside the slave ship. It has treated the immigrant as a threat rather than the stranger Christ commanded us to love. It has used the language of life as a political flag and forgotten the grieving woman behind the statistic. When the church protects only the lives that cost it nothing to protect, it has already betrayed the gospel it claims to carry.

whereWeAgree: Across every honest divide there is one thing we can stand on together. Every human life bears the image of God and possesses a dignity that no one conferred and no one may revoke, from the first hidden cell to the last labored breath.
captureLeft: On the left, the unborn child is the life most easily set aside, spoken of as tissue rather than neighbor, defended in every other case of the voiceless and quietly excepted in this one. A consistency that reaches the prisoner and the refugee but stops at the womb is not yet consistent.
captureRight: On the right, the lives most easily set aside are the born poor, the immigrant at the border, the condemned man in his cell, and the refugee at the door, lives spoken of as burdens or threats. A concern for life that ends at birth and grows cold toward the breathing is not yet a concern for life.
whereWeDiffer: Honest people who hold the same high view of life still differ on the hard cases, on what the law should compel, and on how mercy and justice meet in policy. The rape of a child, the dying mother, the immigration statute, the death penalty, these are places where serious Christians reason in good faith and reach different ends. We can hold the same reverence and still argue about the road.

right.label: Defends the unborn, neglects the life once it is born
right.whatItLooksLike: A fierce and costly devotion to the child in the womb that thins to nothing the moment that child is born poor, or brown, or behind a border, or behind bars. The same voice that calls abortion the great evil of the age will defend the execution of the condemned, the separation of the migrant child from his mother, and the cutting of the bread that keeps the born child alive. Life becomes a single issue rather than a single thread, and the issue is always the one that costs the voter least.
right.inThePast: The modern pro-life movement, as it organized after Roe in 1973, drew its energy from a real conviction that the unborn are neighbors. But it bound itself to a political coalition that also championed the return of the death penalty after Gregg in 1976, the harsh welfare retrenchment of the 1980s and the 1996 reform, and a hard line on the immigrant. The 1980s saw the Moral Majority preach the sanctity of the womb while baptizing an economics indifferent to the mother. The whole life witness was available the entire time and was largely refused.
right.now: The 2018 family separation policy at the southern border was defended or excused by many who name themselves the most pro-life. Capital punishment retains majority support among white evangelicals even as exonerations from the Innocence Project mount and Justice Harry Blackmun's late dissent in Callins haunts the record. Figures such as Robert Jeffress and Franklin Graham have offered theological cover for the harshest border and refugee restrictions, including the 2017 travel ban and reductions in refugee admissions, while abortion is treated as the lone test of a candidate's worth.

left.label: Defends the vulnerable adult, sets aside the unborn
left.whatItLooksLike: A genuine tenderness toward the refugee, the prisoner, and the poor that goes quiet at the womb, where the unborn life is renamed as tissue, a clump of cells, a matter settled by the word choice. Autonomy is raised to an absolute, and the question of whether a second life is present is answered by refusing to ask it. The vulnerable who cannot speak for themselves are defended everywhere except the one place they are smallest.
left.inThePast: The framing hardened over decades. The 1973 settlement treated the unborn as a private matter rather than a public neighbor, and the rhetoric of choice steadily erased the language of the child. NARAL and Planned Parenthood as an advocacy arm moved from the early plea of safe, legal, and rare toward a frame in which the second life is not mentioned at all. The shift was deliberate, and the cost was a vocabulary in which the unborn could no longer be named.
left.now: The push to remove rare from the older formula, and campaigns such as Shout Your Abortion since 2015, mark a frame in which the unborn life is no longer weighed. At the other edge, assisted death has spread, and Canada's MAID regime, expanded in 2021 with a planned track for mental illness, has drawn alarm from disability advocates like the group Not Dead Yet, who document people choosing death for want of housing or care. Prenatal screening has driven Down syndrome to near disappearance in Iceland and Denmark, a quiet verdict on which lives are wanted.

theCost: A consistent ethic of life will cost you your tribe. It will make you suspect to both sides, too pro-life for the one and not pro-life enough for the other, because you refuse to trade the immigrant for the unborn or the unborn for the immigrant. It costs more than a vote. It costs the casserole carried to the frightened pregnant teenager, the visit to the man on death row, the years given to the parent who no longer knows you, the open door to the family who crossed a border. It asks you to be inconvenienced by lives the world has agreed not to see. I have found it easier to hold the right opinion than to answer the phone at two in the morning.
charge: So go and find the edge you have been avoiding. Not the one your tribe already defends, but the one it has taught you to walk past. Learn the name of one life the world has set aside, the unborn or the undocumented, the condemned or the dying, and let that name cost you something this week. The measure of what we believe about the image of God is not the argument we win. It is the body we are willing to carry home in the dark.
